newsitem.title: UK: War crimes suspect was "one of life's survivors".
newsitem.headline: War crimes suspect was "one of life's survivors".

text.p: Szymon Serafinowicz, 86, who was ruled mentally unfit on Friday to stand trial in London on war crimes charges, is a tough, resourceful man whose wartime history reads like an adventure novel.

Serafinowicz and his wife, who died in 1993, were among the few people to walk free from the Nazis' notorious death camp, Dachau. They also escaped the threat of being sent to Siberia after the Soviet Union reclaimed Byelorussia from Nazi Germany.
Like many Byelorussians who loathed their Soviet rulers, Serafinowicz was happy to join a police force set up by the Nazis when they occupied his homeland from 1941 to 1944.
He was quickly promoted to commander of police in the region around the town of Mir in Byelorussia (now the independent state of Belarus).
Serafinowicz was charged with three counts of murdering Jews in the winter of 1941 to 1942, when the Nazis with the local police force wiped out almost all the Jews in Byelorussia.
He denies he took part in the mass slaughter or that he ordered his forces to kill Jews. He says he tried to save them.
When Russia finally drove the Germans out of Byelorussia, Serafinowicz was identified as a collaborator and he and his Polish-born wife Jadwiga were threatened with exile to Siberia.
They fled to France where they surrendered to the Germans, but there was no special treatment from the country Serafinowicz had allied himself with and the couple was sent to Dachau.
Within a week, Serafinowicz had managed to talk his way out of the camp where tens of thousands of people were murdered by the Nazis and he and Jadwiga were free.
Now Serafinowicz switched allegiances, joining General Vladyslav Sikorski's Polish Army in exile. He fought for the Allies in Egypt and Italy.

"In encounters with adversity, he always emerged the right way up. This is a man who knows how to look after himself," prosecuting lawyer Sir Derek Spencer told the court hearing to decide whether Serafinowicz was fit to stand trial.
"He is one of life's survivors," Spencer said.
Serafinowicz and his wife came to Britain after the war and settled in Surrey in southern England.

He found work as a carpenter and bought a small house in the prosperous area of Banstead. They had two sons, Szymon, now 53, and Kazimierz, 50, and to their neighbours they were a quiet, unremarkable family.
Serafinowicz is a tiny man, with a pinched, sunken face and a full head of white hair.
Despite his frail appearance his relatives described him as a tough, stubborn man who dominated even his two tall, sturdy sons. "You could never sway him," said his granddaughter, Helen.

His doctor had to struggle to persuade him to go to hospital when he was seriously ill with shingles and a chest infection late last year. Once there, despite being so sick doctors thought he would die, he at first refused to take any drugs.
Three weeks later, he was fit enough to attend the court.
Serafinowicz had little education. He told police his schooling was disrupted by the Russian revolution and he was taught mainly by an elderly neighbour until he was 13.
He had little time for lessons anyway because his father was a World War One prisoner of war and his mother needed him to help out on the family farm.
Like most people in the region, he spoke Polish, Byelorussian and Russian, but despite spending more than half his life in Britain, he never became fully fluent in English.
Most of his friends in Britain were from Eastern Europe and he never lost his deep affection for his homeland.

His son told the court he had taken a keen interest in news from the former Soviet republic until recent years and Serafinowicz would break into smiles whenever lawyers talked of his life before World War Two.

Serafinowicz's wife died in 1993, shortly after he learned that he was under investigation for war crimes. They had been married for 56 years, and although she had been sick for a long time, he blamed media reports about his case for her death.
